content.text: The text discusses hemorrhagic peritoneal effusion, emphasizing its rarity except in cancer, tuberculosis, acute peritonitis, blood dyscrasias, trauma, ruptured aneurysms, and visceral injuries. It then presents tabes mesenterica as tuberculosis of the mesenteric lymph glands, historically linked with scrofulosis and pulmonary consumption. Most cases occur in children aged two to eight, especially those poorly nourished, artificially fed, or exposed to unhealthy environments. Intestinal inflammation, malnutrition, tuberculosis elsewhere, and possibly infected milk are described as causes. Enlarged glands undergo hyperplasia, caseation, suppuration, calcification, and occasionally rupture. Symptoms include anemia, digestive disturbance, emaciation, abdominal distension, fever, diarrhea or constipation, and sometimes palpable abdominal tumors. Diagnosis depends chiefly on detecting enlarged glands; prognosis is generally unfavorable. Treatment emphasizes prevention, hygiene, nutrition, easily digested food, symptom relief, cod-liver oil, iron, and palliation. An extensive alphabetical index follows.
